prompt: What are the best practices for microservices?
completion:
## Micro‑services Best Practices *(A pragmatic, “run‑the‑world” checklist that covers design, coding, testing, deployment, and ops)* | Area | What to Do | Why It Matters | Quick Tips | |------|------------|----------------|------------| | **1. Domain‑Driven Design (DDD) & Bounded Contexts** | • Split the business domain into *bounded contexts*.
• Map each context to a single service. | Keeps services focused and reduces cross‑cutting concerns. | Use Ubiquitous Language in each context; keep context borders explicit. | | **2. Service Granularity** | • Small, single‑purpose services.
• “One business capability = one service.” | Easier to evolve, deploy, test, and scale. | Avoid “tiny” services that do nothing but delegate; aim for a meaningful unit of work. | | **3. Independence & Autonomy** | • Own data store.
• Independent CI/CD pipeline.
• No shared code that can lock you. | Enables independent versioning and rapid iteration. | Prefer “own‑your‑data” over “share‑your‑data” (except for very well‑defined shared libraries). | | **4. API & Contract Design** | • REST/GraphQL or gRPC APIs.
• Semantic versioning of contracts.
• API gateway for routing & policy enforcement. | Guarantees backward‑compatibility and reduces coupling. | Use OpenAPI/ProtoBuf schemas; run contract tests (e.g., Pact). | | **5. Communication Patterns** | • Synchronous (HTTP/REST, gRPC) for CRUD.
• Asynchronous (AMQP, Kafka, event bus) for state changes & long‑running flows. | Enables resilience and loose coupling. | Make all endpoints idempotent; include correlation IDs. | | **6. Data Management & Consistency** | • Store‑per‑service.
• Use *eventual consistency* & *sagas* for distributed transactions.
• Read‑model CQRS if needed. | Avoids distributed lock headaches; supports horizontal scaling. | Keep eventual‑consistency acceptable for business logic; expose “consistency window” if necessary. | | **7. Resilience & Fault Tolerance** | • Timeout, retry, circuit breaker (Hystrix, Resilience4j, Istio).
• Graceful degradation, fallback logic. | Keeps the system alive under partial failures. | Keep retries idempotent; limit retry count and back‑off. | | **8. Observability** | • Structured logging (ELK, Loki).
• Metrics (Prometheus, StatsD).
• Distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin).
• Alerting (Alertmanager, PagerDuty). | Enables root‑cause analysis and capacity planning. | Log correlation ID; avoid sensitive data in logs. | | **9. Security** | • Mutual TLS for service‑to‑service.
• OAuth2/JWT + scopes.
• Secrets management (Vault, KMS).
• Rate limiting & DoS protection. | Protects data & prevents privilege escalation. | Treat every service as an exposed API; perform penetration tests. | | **10. CI/CD & Automation** | • Git‑based workflow, feature branches.
• Automated tests: unit, integration, contract, end‑to‑end.
• Canary / blue‑green deployments.
• Automated rollback on health‑check failure. | Speeds up releases while keeping quality high. | Use “git‑ops” (ArgoCD, Flux) if running on Kubernetes. | | **11. Governance & Culture** | • Architecture review board (ARB).
• Naming conventions, tagging, service registry.
• Documentation living in code (Swagger, ReDoc). | Reduces drift, knowledge silos, and duplicated effort. | Document decisions in a lightweight, searchable knowledge base. | | **12. Infrastructure & Deployment** | • Containerization (Docker) + orchestration (K8s).
• Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) for traffic control.
• Immutable infrastructure with IaC (Terraform, Pulumi). | Provides scalability, high‑availability, and reproducible environments. | Separate “dev”, “stage”, “prod” namespaces; keep secrets per environment. | | **13. Testing Strategies** | • Unit (fast, isolated).
• Integration (service‑to‑service, DB).
• Contract tests (Pact).
• Chaos engineering (Simian Army, Gremlin).
• Load & performance tests (k6, Gatling). | Identifies issues early, ensures resilience, validates performance. | Run chaos tests in a staging cluster; avoid full‑stack chaos in prod. | | **14. Service Discovery & Load Balancing** | • Use the orchestrator’s native service discovery or Consul/Etcd.
• Client‑side load balancing (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer). | Keeps traffic routing simple and elastic. | Avoid hard‑coded URLs; rely on service names. | | **15. Versioning & Backward Compatibility** | • API major/minor versioning.
• “Deprecated” flags and sunset windows.
• Service contracts via schema registry. | Prevents breaking consumers while evolving services. | Keep old endpoints for at least 2–3 releases before removal. | | **16. Monitoring & Alerting** | • Health endpoints (actuator, readiness/liveness).
• SLA/SLI dashboards (Grafana).
• Alert fatigue mitigation (aggregation, suppression). | Ensures operators know when things go wrong. | Alert on “slow but healthy” metrics, not just 5xx counts. | --- ## How to Use This Checklist 1. **Start with the Domain** Map the business domain → bounded contexts → services. 2. **Define the Contract** Write OpenAPI/ProtoBuf schemas early; run contract tests. 3. **Build & Test** Write unit tests → integration tests → contract tests → chaos tests. 4. **Automate the Pipeline** Build → test → deploy (canary) → monitor → rollback if needed. 5. **Observe & Improve** Use metrics & traces to detect bottlenecks. Iterate on data models, APIs, and patterns. --- ## Quick Reference Cheat Sheet | ✅ Item | ✔️ Done? | 📦 Tool | 📖 Reading | |---------|----------|---------|------------| | Service per Bounded Context | | | “Domain‑Driven Design” by Evans | | Own your database | | | “Microservices Patterns” by Sam Newman | | Idempotent endpoints | | | “Designing Data-Intensive Applications” | | Circuit breaker | | Resilience4j, Istio | | | Tracing with correlation ID | | Jaeger, OpenTelemetry | | | Mutual TLS | | Istio, Linkerd | | | Canary deployments | | Argo Rollouts, Flagger | | | Chaos experiments | | Gremlin, Litmus | | | API contract tests | | Pact, Contract Testing | | --- ### Common Anti‑Patterns to Avoid | Anti‑Pattern | Why It’s Bad | Remedy | |--------------|--------------|--------| | “Service Monolith” – too many small services | Increases overhead, makes tracing hard | Re‑bound to a smaller set of cohesive services | | Tight coupling through shared databases | Breaks isolation | Adopt event‑driven sync; move to per‑service DB | | “Golden Ticket” (single admin service) | Single point of failure | Split admin into domain‑specific services | | No versioning or contract tests | Breaks consumer apps | Use schema registry + contract tests | | Ignoring resilience (no retries, circuit breaker) | System dies under load | Add retry/back‑off, circuit breaker | | “In‑house” infrastructure management | Hides complexity, hard to scale | Use managed Kubernetes, Cloud‑native tooling | --- ## Final Thought Micro‑services are not just a technology choice—they’re a **design mindset**. Start simple, iterate fast, and treat each service as a first‑class citizen with its own data, API, and deployment pipeline. Follow the checklist, keep the principles in mind, and your system will evolve gracefully, remain resilient, and stay aligned with business goals.
